source: Gandhi et al. (2025) BoxingGym: Benchmarking Progress in Automated Experimental Design and Model Discovery
finding: Ten simulated science worlds where an LLM picks experiments, then predicts. All tested models, open and closed, struggle at both choosing informative experiments and discovering models.
numbers: 10 environments; 5 runs; scores at 0,1,3,5,7,10 experiments; experiment quality = Expected Information Gain (EIG) regret vs best of 100 random experiments; GPT-4o had lowest EIG regret; 32B models beat 7B in the same family
quote: all current approaches struggle with both experimental design and model discovery
limits: Simulated generative models, not real labs. Small model set (GPT-4o, Qwen2.5, OpenThinker).
agent_relevance: Gives a measurable score for S4 test design: EIG regret. We can score our agent's chosen tests the same way.

source: Gandhi et al. (2025) BoxingGym, prior-knowledge condition
finding: Giving the model domain context did not help. After 10 experiments models often did better with no prior description. Strong early assumptions were not revised; in hyperbolic discounting, error rose with more experiments.
numbers: prior vs no-prior compared in 3 environments (population growth, IRT, hyperbolic discounting); error bars = SE over 5 runs
limits: Only a few environments show it; mechanism (overfit to few points) is the authors' reading.
agent_relevance: Supports G1/G3: a model's confident prior can freeze test design. Tests should be chosen to break the prior, not confirm it.

source: Gandhi et al. (2025) BoxingGym, Box's Apprentice and explanation tests
finding: Adding an explicit statistical-model-fitting tool (Box's Apprentice) did not reliably beat plain GPT-4o; it chose too-simple forms like linear fits. A novice (GPT-4o) given the scientist's written explanation did worse than the scientist who ran the experiments.
numbers: novice always gpt-4o; explanation quality better with 32B than 7B scientist; helped in animal growth, poor in moral judgment
limits: Qualitative reading of why the tool failed.
agent_relevance: Handing a tool to the model is not enough. Written notes lose part of what experiments taught; keep raw outputs, not only summaries, in memory.

source: Huang et al. (2025) POPPER: Automated Hypothesis Validation with Agentic Sequential Falsifications
finding: Two LLM agents design and run falsification tests; e-values combine evidence with strict Type-I error control. Most baselines (ReAct, Self-Refine, LLM likelihood ratio) failed to hold false-positive rate at 0.1 on at least one set. POPPER held it by the paper's rule and had higher power.
numbers: alpha=0.1; Type-I on DiscoveryBench: POPPER 0.152, ReAct 0.145, Self-Refine 0.248; POPPER power 0.610 DiscoveryBench, 0.897 TargetVal-IL2, 0.717 IFNG (the last row of the extracted table is hard to align, so check against the PDF); negatives built by column permutation (50 negatives for target validation, 20 positives); 5 runs
limits: Type-I control is on permutation nulls, judged within 1 SD of alpha. Small target-validation positive set (20). Table text was garbled in extraction, so some cells may be misaligned.
agent_relevance: Direct template for S4: negative controls made by permuting data, plus a statistical stopping rule. Matches Hacking-style use of controls.

source: Huang et al. (2025) POPPER, ablations
finding: Removing the relevance checker (does the test really bear on the hypothesis) raises false positives. A plain code-generation executor inside POPPER was worse than a ReAct one.
numbers: POPPER-CodeGen Type-I 0.311/0.264/0.173 on the three sets; text says NoReleCheck 'significantly raises' Type-I
limits: Relevance checker is itself an LLM; its errors not measured separately here.
agent_relevance: A check that a test actually tests the claim (not a side fact) must be a separate step before running it.

source: Huang et al. (2025) POPPER, human expert study
finding: Nine computational biologists did the same validation on TargetVal-IL2. POPPER matched them in power and error with no significant difference, and ran faster with more tests.
numbers: 9 experts; POPPER 9.7x faster, 3.6x more lines of code, 2.5x more statistical tests
limits: Very small human sample; no significant difference is weak evidence of equality.
agent_relevance: Shows a scaffolded loop can match experts on test execution speed; the gain is in breadth of tests, not judgement.

source: Jansen et al. (2024) DiscoveryWorld: A Virtual Environment for Developing and Evaluating Automated Scientific Discovery Agents
finding: 120 tasks in 8 topics, three difficulty levels. Strong agents (ReAct, Plan+Execute, Hypothesizer) did poorly end to end, while doing moderately on unit tasks like using one instrument.
numbers: best completion: ReAct 38% easy, 18% challenge; best explanatory knowledge (Hypothesizer) 34% easy, 8% challenge; unit tests 60%+ completion; 5 parametric seeds per task; easy tasks 100 steps, others 1000
limits: Text simulation; three baseline agents only; GPT-4o era models.
agent_relevance: Skills (measuring) work, chaining them into a designed experiment does not. Suggests S4 needs explicit stage control from code.

source: Jansen et al. (2024) DiscoveryWorld, human scientists
finding: Expert human scientists solved most tasks, though some challenge tasks were solved by only one person. When stuck, humans sometimes brute-forced and got the answer without the explanation.
numbers: average completion 66%; 11 of 16 human task sets above 60%; explanatory knowledge 55%
limits: 16 task sets, few participants, mixed expertise.
agent_relevance: The completion-vs-explanation gap is a warning: a passing result without the mechanism should not count as a finding (G3).

source: Choudhury et al. (2026) BED-LLM: Intelligent Information Gathering with LLMs and Bayesian Experimental Design (ICLR 2026)
finding: Code computes expected information gain over the LLM's own answer predictions and picks the question; this more than doubled 20-Questions success in most setups vs prompting the LLM to ask good questions.
numbers: mean +37.4 percentage points over Prompt-Only; Animals GPT-4o 45% to 93%; Celebrities Mistral-Large 19% to 91%; Things GPT-4o 34% to 64%; 100 targets per set; six LLMs
limits: 20 Questions and movie preferences only; answerer simulated by an LLM; several LLM calls per turn.
agent_relevance: Strongest direct evidence for G5-style design: the program ranks candidate tests by EIG, the model only proposes them.

source: Choudhury et al. (2026) BED-LLM, ablations
finding: Parts matter. Using the LLM's raw in-context belief update instead of a filtered Bayesian one hurt badly; predictive entropy alone was weaker than full EIG; asking the LLM to pick the best question by judgment (Implicit Max) was weaker than full EIG.
numbers: Animals GPT-4o: BED-LLM 93, Entropy 88, Data-Estimation 70, ICL Beliefs 25, Implicit Max 70; Things Llama-3.1-8B: BED-LLM 26, Entropy 15, Data-Est 9, ICL 11, Implicit 10
limits: Ablations on one game family.
agent_relevance: Do not trust the model to update beliefs in context after a test. Keep the hypothesis set and filter it in code.

source: Beel, Kan, Baumgart (2025) Evaluating Sakana's AI Scientist: Bold Claims, Mixed Results, and a Promising Future?
finding: Independent test of the AI Scientist on 12 ideas. Five failed on coding errors. Runs that finished often had broken experiments, such as a parameter that never varied and a baseline that was not rerun.
numbers: 5 of 12 failed (42%); 7 manuscripts; code grew 8% in first iteration (529 of 6,260 chars) then 118, 83, 66, 21; 4 of 7 manuscripts (57%) had wrong or hallucinated numbers; 5 of 34 citations from 2020 or later; cost $6-15 per paper
limits: Small sample (12 ideas), template-based ML tasks; evaluation by the authors.
agent_relevance: Classic experimental-practice failure: no check that the manipulation took effect or that the control ran. Add manipulation checks and baseline reruns in code.

source: Lu et al. (2024) The AI Scientist: Towards Fully Automated Open-Ended Scientific Discovery
finding: Agent loop: idea, experiment plan, code edit via Aider, run, notes in a journal, up to 5 experiment iterations, retry up to 4 times on errors. Authors admit it may implement ideas wrongly and cannot control parameters, FLOPs or runtime fairly.
numbers: cost under $15 per paper; automated reviewer review cost $0.25-0.50; paper reports reviewer F1 0.57 on NeurIPS consistency data
limits: Authors' own system and own reviewer; limited experiments per idea.
agent_relevance: The authors name the fairness-of-comparison problem. A matched-budget baseline (G7) must be part of every test the agent designs.

source: Yamada et al. (2025) The AI Scientist-v2: Workshop-Level Automated Scientific Discovery via Agentic Tree Search
finding: Tree search over experiments plus a vision-language feedback step. Three fully AI-written papers went to an ICLR workshop; one was above the acceptance bar. Its result was negative (the regularizer did not help).
numbers: 3 submitted; accepted paper scores 6, 7, 6 (mean 6.33), about top 45% of submissions
limits: 3 papers; workshop for negative results (ICBINB); one success; reviewers knew some papers were AI-made.
agent_relevance: Branching over experiment variants with code-side selection works at workshop level; claims of discovery still need human checks.

source: Starace et al. (2025) PaperBench: Evaluating AI's Ability to Replicate AI Research
finding: Agents must rebuild and run experiments from 20 ICML 2024 papers. Best was Claude 3.5 Sonnet at 21.0%; ML PhDs beat the model on a 3-paper subset.
numbers: 20 papers, 8,316 rubric items; BasicAgent: Claude 3.5 Sonnet 21.0, o1-high 13.2, DeepSeek-R1 6.0, GPT-4o 4.1, Gemini 2.0 Flash 3.2, o3-mini-high 2.6; humans 41.4% (best of 3, 48 hours) vs o1 26.6% on 3 papers; Code-Dev variant o1 43.4%
limits: Rubric graded by an LLM judge (o3-mini, F1 0.83, about $66 per paper); 12-hour agent limit.
agent_relevance: Replication is the discipline in the Galison/Hacking story. Running and getting results, not writing code, is where the gap lies (Code-Dev 43.4% vs full run).

source: Starace et al. (2025) PaperBench, scaffold sensitivity
finding: A prompt scaffold (IterativeAgent: cannot end early, works piecewise) raised o3-mini-high and hurt Claude 3.5 Sonnet.
numbers: IterativeAgent: o3-mini-high 8.5 (vs 2.6 BasicAgent), Claude 3.5 Sonnet 16.1 (vs 21.0)
limits: Single scaffold change; 3 runs per paper.
agent_relevance: The same scaffold helps one model and hurts another. Test the scaffold on the actual model (G7).

source: Chan et al. (2024) MLE-bench: Evaluating Machine Learning Agents on Machine Learning Engineering
finding: 75 Kaggle competitions; best setup (o1-preview with AIDE) reached bronze or better in 16.9%. More attempts and more time helped.
numbers: o1-preview 16.9% pass@1 to 34.1% pass@8; GPT-4o 8.7% with 24 hours, 11.8% with more time; 24-hour runs
limits: Kaggle tasks with a clear leaderboard metric; contamination checked by the authors.
agent_relevance: A hidden test metric and held-out score is the model for G3. Gains from repeat trials show how noisy single runs are.

source: Huang et al. (2024) MLAgentBench: Evaluating Language Agents on Machine Learning Experimentation
finding: 13 ML experimentation tasks with a ReAct agent. Success depends on whether the task is old (likely in training data) or new.
numbers: Claude v3 Opus agent 37.5% average success (improve metric by 10% over starter); 100% on house-price, 0% on some recent Kaggle tasks
limits: Success threshold is only +10% over baseline; setting is ML tuning, not hypothesis testing.
agent_relevance: Possible contamination: apparent skill on familiar tasks may be memory. Use novel or mutated tasks to test design skill.

source: Yiu, Kosoy, Gopnik (2023) Imitation versus Innovation: What children can do that large language and language-and-vision models cannot (yet)?
finding: Children aged 3-7 found novel tool uses and blicket causal structure from a few trials. GPT, PaLM and LaMDA, given the children's data in words, did much worse on causal structure and on choosing a novel functional tool.
numbers: children n=42; children 88.4% (SE 2.82) vs adults 84.9% (SE 3.07) on one tool task; 85.2% vs adults 95.7% on the unrelated-object task; LLM scores are in figures I did not read
limits: Position paper; prompt format may disadvantage LLMs; older models.
agent_relevance: Active intervention to tell hypotheses apart is a known weak spot for LLMs; a scaffold must supply the discriminating test.

source: Alderete and Baker (2026 preprint, under review) Separable Pathways for Causal Reasoning: Architectural Scaffolding for Hypothesis-Space Restructuring in LLM Agents
finding: Blicket-detector task with a rule switch mid-game. Scaffold with typed state machines (context graphs, CG) plus runtime monitors (dynamic behaviors, DB) helped. CG gave 94% of the accuracy gain in the post-switch space; monitors caught regime change.
numbers: 1,085 trials; raw accuracy Base 87.3%, CG 77.3%, CG+DB 89.1% (Fisher p=0.015 one-tailed, CG+DB vs CG); reasoning-eligible accuracy Base 97.5, CG 98.7, CG+DB 97.9; CG+DB costs 30-50% more; monitor sensitivity 100% across 5 datasets
limits: Own task variants and own scaffold, preprint not peer reviewed; CG alone numerically worse than Base on raw accuracy (not significant); batch variance high.
agent_relevance: Supports a code-side detector that fires on surprising evidence (impasse) and expands the hypothesis set. Gains are modest and single-lab.

source: Search snippets: Kosoy et al. (2022) blicket environment for RL agents; adults vs LLMs on free blicket intervention (eScholarship)
finding: From search snippets only: LLMs can match adults on some blicket hypothesis inference but explore less efficiently, and show a conjunctive vs disjunctive rule gap.
numbers: not read
limits: Not opened; verify before use.
agent_relevance: Pointer for a later pass on LLM intervention choice.

source: King et al. (2009) The Automation of Science (Robot Scientist Adam)
finding: Older AI system closing the loop in a lab: hypothesis, experiment on a robot, analysis, new hypothesis, for yeast gene function. Cited from memory; not opened this session.
numbers: not verified here
limits: Not opened; numbers deliberately left out.
agent_relevance: Early example that a symbolic planner plus a physical lab can run the whole experiment cycle; LLM-era versions replace the planner.

source: Cross-reading: BED-LLM vs BoxingGym
finding: Both papers agree: an LLM left to choose experiments on judgment alone is poor; code-computed information gain fixes much of it. BoxingGym uses EIG only as a score, BED-LLM uses it to choose.
numbers: BED-LLM +37.4 pp mean; BoxingGym EIG regret ranks models but no selector tested
limits: Different tasks; no head-to-head run.
agent_relevance: Test selection by EIG in code is the strongest tested lever; running it on BoxingGym is a cheap next experiment.

source: Cross-reading: POPPER, Beel et al., AI Scientist
finding: Three failure types recur: tests that do not bear on the claim (POPPER relevance ablation), manipulations that did not take effect (Beel: fixed parameter), and missing baseline reruns (Beel).
numbers: Beel 5/12 runs failed, 4/7 papers had wrong numbers; POPPER NoReleCheck raises Type-I
limits: Synthesis by this agent, across papers with different setups.
agent_relevance: Gives three code-checkable gates for S4: relevance, manipulation check, control rerun.

source: Cross-reading: scaffold sensitivity across studies
finding: Scaffold effects are model specific and sometimes negative: IterativeAgent hurt Claude 3.5 Sonnet (21.0 to 16.1) but helped o3-mini-high (2.6 to 8.5); CG alone lowered raw accuracy in the blicket study (87.3 to 77.3).
numbers: see c15, c19
limits: Synthesis; different tasks.
agent_relevance: Reinforces G7: measure every added step at equal tokens on our model.

source: Cross-reading: DiscoveryWorld unit tests vs full tasks
finding: Instrument-level skill is not the bottleneck. The bottleneck is coupling design, control and interpretation across steps.
numbers: unit tests 60%+ vs full-task 38% easy / 18% challenge for ReAct
limits: Synthesis; one benchmark.
agent_relevance: The scaffold's value is in sequencing S4 steps (control, manipulation check, held-out read-out), not in teaching single skills.

source: Gap note: no study found of LLMs doing Hacking-style instrument calibration or Galison-style cross-community trading
finding: In the sources opened here, none tests whether an agent checks that its instrument works (known-answer test) before trusting a result. DiscoveryWorld unit tasks come closest.
numbers: none
limits: Absence of evidence from limited search (3 web searches plus direct arXiv fetches); not proof nothing exists.
agent_relevance: Open item: build a known-answer test into S4 and measure it ourselves.
